title: Organised crime on the high street, in rural areas and online
label: 18 November 2026 · Policing and organised crime
summary: The committee questioned the Policing Minister and Home Office officials about how organised crime affects shops, rural communities and online markets. Ministers described raids, better information-sharing and plans to reorganise policing, but members pressed them on whether neighbourhood officers were genuinely additional, whether successful local projects had enough money, and how reforms would protect local knowledge. The Minister said several responses were still being developed, including the high-street crackdown and an update to the drugs strategy.

glossary.definition: A UK agency that investigates serious and organised crime, including crimes crossing local or national borders.
Council teams that enforce rules on goods and businesses, including the sale of illegal products.
An approach in which police remove criminals from an area, prevent their return, and work with others to improve the area over time.
Drug-dealing networks that move drugs between areas, often exploiting children or vulnerable people.
Powerful laboratory-made drugs that can cause fatal overdoses.
Taking money or property obtained through crime away from criminals.
The UK regulator responsible for enforcing rules on online services, among other communications services.
A UK law that places duties on online services to address illegal content and other specified harms.

chapters.title: Finding the pattern behind local crime
chapters.takeaway: National information can reveal links between local incidents, but the Minister said police systems and knowledge of emerging crimes need improvement.

turns.speaker: Dr Prinsley
turns.text: Where are the main gaps in what the Home Office knows about organised crime, and how will it get a better national picture?

evidence.quote: What does the Home Office see as the key gaps in the understanding of serious and organised crime threats? What plans are there to have a better national understanding of this problem?

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones
turns.text: Crime changes quickly, particularly as criminals use new technology. The National Crime Agency draws on police information and other sources, including wastewater surveys, to judge threats and decide what needs attention. But we're still at an early stage in understanding how organised groups are connected to suspicious vape shops and other businesses on struggling high streets.

evidence.quote: serious and organised crime is extremely wide-ranging and constantly changing.
the National Crime Agency will gather information from across a range of different sources—not just from their own intelligence but from policing or surveys, such as waste water surveys.
our evidence and intelligence around what is joining up some of the OCGs that are involved are at the early stages.

turns.speaker: Dr Prinsley
turns.text: We saw a police programme bringing together information from many places. Are we investing enough in the technology to do that nationally, and can officers dealing with a shop on the street get the information they need?

evidence.quote: the way in which it was using technology to interpret data that was coming from all over the place.
are we investing the right amount of money in the right stuff to help us do this?
How do they get what they need to know when they are dealing with the criminals in front of them?

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones
turns.text: First we have to fix old police computer systems that don't work well together; otherwise AI can't analyse the combined information properly. Criminals are also finding new ways to bring in drugs, including disguising them as other products, so detection technology has to keep up.

evidence.quote: we have a lot of old systems that do not necessarily speak to each other in the way that they should, so we are investing quite a lot of money in those systems to make sure that the datasets can be analysed with AI. But you have to fix the datasets first
the drugs are the boxes of bananas. They are literally being turned into new products, so we have to have the technology to find them.

turns.speaker: Rod McLean
turns.text: The National Crime Agency has also received a budget of close to £1.1 billion this year, 19% above 2024–25. A lot of that is intended to improve its technology.

evidence.quote: It had a record funding settlement this year, giving it a budget of close to £1.1 billion—a 19% increase on 2024-25—and a lot of that is to invest in improvements to its technology.

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones
turns.text: A suspicious shop might involve illegal employment, illicit goods or money laundering. Police need to work with trading standards, tax officials and the body that registers companies. Bringing them together around a specific operation is easier than making information flow reliably across every kind of crime. That's one reason I want to reorganise policing.

evidence.quote: It may be selling illicit goods; it may be money laundering—it could be doing a range of criminal activity. You need all the agencies to work together.
It has to go beyond policing to trading standards, HMRC, Companies House—all of those. The information flows have to be there.
The challenge for us is how we do that across all crime types. That is one of the most powerful reasons why we believe we need to fundamentally reform the policing system

turns.speaker: David Grahame
turns.text: We've seen a useful pattern with other crimes: a national team spots connections that individual areas might miss, then sends that information back to local teams so they can act.

evidence.quote: Getting that pattern at the national level and seeing beyond what is happening in local areas, but then being able to push that information back out to particular local areas to take action seems to be a model that is pretty effective across multiple crime types and threat types.

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones
turns.text: Even if some crime figures are falling, the things people see locally—shop theft, antisocial behaviour and suspicious shops—have been going the wrong way. Years of declining neighbourhood policing have left a gap, so we need to protect it.

evidence.quote: the crime types that the public are most likely to observe have been going in the wrong direction. Shop theft, antisocial behaviour, the vape shops
the collapse of neighbourhood policing over many years has led to a real gap.

chapters.title: Officers, local projects and difficult trade-offs
chapters.takeaway: More officers are working in neighbourhoods, but members challenged whether that increases the total workforce or moves gaps elsewhere.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We've heard that forced labour can occur throughout a business's supply chain. When policies change—for example, rules on vape packaging—does the Home Office check whether they could increase or reduce that exploitation?

evidence.quote: We have had evidence throughout this inquiry that there is forced labour in every bit of the supply chain.
When you are changing policies—for example, on plain packaging on vapes—do you do an analysis of what that might do to levels of exploitation and forced labour?

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones
turns.text: I can take away the question about assessing that packaging policy. More generally, we're training neighbourhood officers to recognise exploitation, and it's part of our work on county lines and suspicious shops.

evidence.quote: We can take that away.
One element of that is about serious and organised crime and vulnerability, and to know when exploitation is there when you see it.
there is the county lines programme
There will be an exploitation strand in the work on vape shops.

turns.speaker: Matt Bishop
turns.text: Neighbourhood police numbers have risen, but the overall police workforce has fallen. Was the plan to move people out of other jobs, and could that leave those jobs short-staffed?

evidence.quote: the workforce has gone down within the police overall. Was that the Government’s intention?
Are you concerned that your ambitions for safer high streets and other such projects may be undermined if investigative capacity is undermined in any way?

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones
turns.text: Police chiefs asked us to remove funding rules that encouraged them to keep officers in office jobs even when police staff could do those jobs for less. Chiefs can now choose their mix of officers and staff. Some neighbourhood officers are new recruits; others have moved from elsewhere. I don't yet know whether overall numbers will fall further—that depends on future spending decisions.

evidence.quote: they were maintaining officer levels, but they were then cutting police staff and putting those officers into back-office jobs that should be done by police staff, often for less cost.
Some of them are new and some of them are redeployed.
We have not made any decisions about how we do that, so we will have those conversations with the Treasury.

turns.speaker: Robbie Moore
turns.text: Of the promised 13,000 additional neighbourhood police, how many so far are genuinely new recruits rather than officers moved from other roles? If an officer moves, are you checking what happens to their old job?

evidence.quote: how many of the 13,000 are new recruits so far?
If we are moving a police officer from a job to do neighbourhood policing, is the Home Office looking at the impact that is having on the previous role that the officer was doing?

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones
turns.text: We don't have a figure separating new recruits from those moved into neighbourhood policing. We're tracking how many people work there, and we monitor how forces perform across crimes. I wouldn't expect other services to suffer, but chiefs decide how to organise their staff. The total number of police has gone down.

evidence.quote: We have not got that figure.
We are monitoring how the police are doing across the board
I would certainly not expect other services to be detrimentally impacted
The police chief has to manage his or her workforce
It has gone down, yes.

turns.speaker: Robbie Moore
turns.text: Clear, Hold, Build reduced theft and similar crimes in its trial. If it works, why doesn't the Home Office give it dedicated funding, especially when keeping an area free of crime and rebuilding it takes resources?

evidence.quote: Given that it is considered a success, why are the Government not funding it?
The Hold and Build parts have been identified as being a bit more challenging, but why would the Government not allocate ringfenced funding

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones
turns.text: The trials showed roughly a 23% to 24% fall in theft and similar crimes. But it works best where police, councils and community groups all commit, and rebuilding is the hardest part. Apart from one exception, this work has always come from local police budgets. I encourage forces to use it where it fits, rather than require it everywhere.

evidence.quote: in the main, there was quite a large reduction in acquisitive crime—about 23% or 24%
The Build bit is the trickiest: you need buy-in from lots of different organisations
We would expect it to come out of local police budgets
I have not instructed them to, but the evaluation is certainly positive, and I would encourage forces to use it.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Members have seen this work locally and been impressed. But removing criminals may take weeks, while rebuilding a place can take years. Will you seek funding specifically for that longer phase?

evidence.quote: Clear is a few weeks; Hold is a few weeks; Build is years.
are the Government considering putting a funding review bid in for build support

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones
turns.text: I don't know yet what we'll ask for in the next spending review. The longer phase can involve much more than policing: helping young people avoid crime, tackling underlying problems and finding viable businesses to occupy shops after criminals leave. It needs investment.

evidence.quote: I do not know what is going to be in our spending review bid yet.
the work that they do around trying to stop young people getting involved in crime could be called Build.
you have to fill the shops with viable businesses.
that last bit is always the hardest and involves investment.

chapters.title: Stopping criminal businesses reopening
chapters.takeaway: The high-street crackdown has seized money and raided shops, but officials said they still need to identify the networks behind them and prevent them reopening elsewhere.

turns.speaker: Preet Kaur Gill
turns.text: The high-street operation has visited or raided thousands of premises and made arrests. How many arrests led to charges, and how many of those charged ran or financed the networks?

evidence.quote: Operation Machinize—saw 3,029 premises visited or raided and made 349 arrests. How many of those arrests have led to charges and how many of those charged are alleged to have run or financed the networks?

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones
turns.text: I don't have the number charged. My arrest figure is 232, which differs from the one you've given. The operation seized £2.2 million in cash and £6.8 million in other assets, froze accounts worth £3.7 million and identified £4.2 million in tax evasion. But that's only part of the problem.

evidence.quote: For arrests, we have 232. But I do not know how many of those have been subsequently charged.

Some £2.2 million in cash was seized; £3.7 million worth of accounts were frozen; £4.2 million of tax evasion was identified as part of that op; and £6.8 million of non-cash assets were seized as well.
that is the tip of the iceberg.

turns.speaker: Preet Kaur Gill
turns.text: If a closed shop reopens under the same people in another council area, how will the new area's police and trading standards know? And how is the £30 million for this crackdown divided?

evidence.quote: when a shop is closed and the same people reopen in another council area, who takes the lead in following that up? How are police and trading standards in the new area alerted?
of the £30 million that has been announced for the high street organised crime crackdown, how much is actually going to council trading standards teams?

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones
turns.text: We're still working out how to stop shops simply moving. We need to investigate the criminal groups behind them, not just raid individual premises, and make it harder to open such shops in the first place. Of the £30 million, £6 million goes to trading standards and £20 million to the National Crime Agency and wider law enforcement, with some support for tax and immigration enforcement.

evidence.quote: We need to move from a programme where we raid individual shops to understanding what the serious organised crime element is and how it all joins up. How exactly do we stop displacement into other areas?
how we try to make it harder for criminal gangs to open such shops in the first place
£6 million of that is trading standards, and £20 million is for the NCA and law enforcement more widely, with some support for HMRC and immigration enforcement, as well.

turns.speaker: David Grahame
turns.text: We're moving from counting raids towards asking whether we're stopping the groups behind the shops. Longer shop-closure powers are another way to seek a lasting result, rather than a series of separate raids.

evidence.quote: we are at the stage of moving from activity to how we get to outcomes more
the patterns and groups behind, and how we can better identify those and go against them more systematically.
There are also the systemic changes, like closure orders

turns.speaker: Robbie Moore
turns.text: West Yorkshire has serious problems with suspicious shops. Keighley alone has had 20 premises raided this year. Why wasn't West Yorkshire chosen as one of the three main areas receiving this funding?

evidence.quote: West Yorkshire trading standards raided 20 premises in Keighley this year alone
why was West Yorkshire not considered as one of the three target areas by the Government?

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones
turns.text: The intelligence identified the West Midlands, Greater Manchester, and Kent and Essex as the areas of greatest risk. Other forces can apply to the National Crime Agency for money. That doesn't mean West Yorkshire isn't a priority or that its police can't run their own operations; I can find out what the trading standards funding means for West Yorkshire.

evidence.quote: There are three areas that we are particularly targeting: West Midlands, Greater Manchester, and Kent and Essex police.
Police forces across the country can also bid into the NCA for resources
No, that is not what I am saying. I am saying that there is a fund that West Yorkshire police can bid into.
I can find out for you what that means in terms of West Yorkshire
That is not to say that our police forces will not be able to work with partners to do their own raids in their own areas.

turns.speaker: Ben Maguire
turns.text: Raids happen after a business has opened. What about the accountants, solicitors, banks and others that may help these businesses operate? What are you doing to prevent them opening?

evidence.quote: They have things such as professional services, accountants, solicitors’ firms and, in some cases, banks transferring funds.
What is the Home Office doing to tackle all those problems—which could actually stop these businesses in the first place?

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones
turns.text: That's right: we need to do more before a shop opens, including sharing what councils, tax officials and the company register know, and looking at landlords' responsibilities. Councils' trading standards teams have lost resources over many years. We're also changing the law to allow a shop to be closed for up to a year, but we may need to go further.

evidence.quote: What more can we do on the ownership of some of those buildings, and on making people responsible for who they are letting their shops to?
Companies House, HMRC and all these different agencies have bits of information, and we could be much better at sharing it
Trading standards resources in local authorities, as we know, have been hollowed out over many years
you can close a shop for a year
do we need to go further? Yes

chapters.title: Rural crime and the shape of police reform
chapters.takeaway: The Minister argued that local forces should fund much rural policing, while members worried that limited resources and larger police structures could weaken local expertise.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Rural crime can fall between local police, who may lack specialist knowledge, and regional organised-crime teams, who may see it as too small. Is the Home Office looking at that problem?

evidence.quote: maybe it was too low level for the ROCUs but local policing did not know enough about it.
Are you specifically looking at rural crime in the Home Office?

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones
turns.text: Yes. Rural crime isn't recorded as one single category, which can make patterns harder to see. Waste crime, for example, grew before it became a national priority. Officers need to understand rural offences, while dedicated teams and trusted relationships with farmers can help people feel it's worth reporting them.

evidence.quote: Because rural crime is not defined—the datasets, as you know, are by crime type rather than the type of area that they fall within
It was not seen as a national priority quickly enough, but it now is
training officers to understand what rural crime is.
have a relationship with farmers who trust that something will be done so actually report the crime.

turns.speaker: Ben Maguire
turns.text: The national rural crime unit gets £800,000, but a force such as Devon and Cornwall has vast areas to cover. Is that amount enough, and will funding account for the cost of policing rural places?

evidence.quote: my Devon and Cornwall force would be quite concerned to hear that because, as far as I know, it does not receive any additional funding for the rurality aspect of what it has to police.
do you really think that £800,000 is proportionate to the cost of rural policing in our country?

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones
turns.text: The £800,000 supports a targeted national unit; most rural policing is paid for from each force's wider budget. I expect forces to cover rural crime, though some do it better than others. I'm also reviewing how police funding is calculated, including whether it reflects rural geography and seasonal changes.

evidence.quote: you get a lot of value for what is actually a relatively small amount of Government investment—£800,000.
Within that budget, the police make decisions about what they prioritise and what they do not, and I expect them to cover rural crime in their budgets
Other areas do it less well.
I am doing a lot of work to review the funding formula.
rurality, seasonality—all these things.

turns.speaker: Rod McLean
turns.text: There is £45 million over three years for the Environment Agency to tackle illegal waste sites. Police and the National Crime Agency are supporting its investigations. A joint national team is also being tried in Greater Manchester and West Yorkshire, but any wider rollout would need evaluation.

evidence.quote: There is £45 million over three years for the Environment Agency to tackle the sites
The NCA is leaning in to support the Environment Agency with mentoring and intelligence support.
It includes the Environment Agency, the police, the NCA and a range of other partners. That approach is now being trialled in Greater Manchester and West Yorkshire.
subject to evaluation, of course.

turns.speaker: Robbie Moore
turns.text: The law intended to prevent theft of equipment such as quad bikes was passed in 2023. When will the detailed rules needed to put it into effect arrive, and why have immobilisers been dropped from the proposals?

evidence.quote: We are three years down the line from this legislation being introduced. A lot of quad bikes and ATVs are stolen as part of serious and organised crime within rural areas
When will that be presented to the House? Why have the Government dropped immobilisers from their proposals?

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones
turns.text: We've run into legal and vehicle-registration issues, including how rules would affect manufacturers and imports. I want the rules in place quickly and hope to introduce them by early next year, but resolving those issues has been difficult.

evidence.quote: We have bumped up against complex legal trade vehicle registration issues.
we need to make sure that that fits with the law and with WTO law. There is a whole raft of complexity around it.
Hopefully by early next year.

turns.speaker: Robbie Moore
turns.text: Regional organised-crime units can help local forces, but local areas don't always feel supported. What will happen to those units under your proposed police reforms, and how will you preserve what works?

evidence.quote: local areas do not always feel well supported by their regional organised crime units.
How will the Government ensure that they remain effective when they are encompassed within a larger police force structure?

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones
turns.text: The regional units do good work, but their funding depends partly on local forces, and their staff are borrowed from those forces. We want a more reliable arrangement: national work would sit in a proposed national police service, with regional specialist work in new bodies. We'd introduce changes gradually rather than move major crime functions before the new service can handle them.

evidence.quote: they are funded by local forces and the Home Office.
all the staff in ROCUs are seconded from local forces.
The national-facing resources will sit within the national police service, and then the more regional will sit within the new bodies.
we start small with the national police service and we build out; we do not add serious and organised crime, the National Crime Agency or CT until it is load bearing

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The Home Secretary has announced 200 local policing areas. If areas and specialist teams get bigger, how will officers retain knowledge of places such as neighbouring parts of Staffordshire, Cheshire and Derbyshire? I don't want to lose a commander who knows my own district.

evidence.quote: The Home Secretary has today announced 200 local policing areas.
they simply won’t understand the bit of England that I represent and that is represented by MPs in Derbyshire and Cheshire.
You are telling me that I might have a commander at the north Staffordshire level and not at the Moorlands level, and that is worse for me.

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones
turns.text: Local officers must understand their areas, build relationships and pass information to specialists when needed. The 200 areas' exact boundaries haven't been settled. Each is meant to have a commander with real authority, while smaller neighbourhood teams and a named local officer remain. We have to make sure national reform doesn't weaken local policing.

evidence.quote: local police understand their local area and that they are able to police it, have relationships, build intelligence and feed that up the system
they took their eye off the ball on local policing. We have to not do that.
the exact geography is TBC
Yes.
We need to know who your named local officer is.
the idea is that you have a proper commander with proper authority over a local area.

chapters.title: Drugs, treatment and criminal profits
chapters.takeaway: The Minister favoured updating the existing drugs strategy rather than replacing it, while members questioned demand, prevention and how much criminal money is recovered.

turns.speaker: Preet Kaur Gill
turns.text: What does the review of the drugs strategy mean? With cocaine production high and new drugs appearing, what evidence shows the Government is shrinking the market that criminal groups profit from?

evidence.quote: the Government are saying they are reviewing the drug strategy. Can you tell us what that means?
What evidence do you have that the Government are shrinking the market that these gangs profit from?

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones
turns.text: The existing approach—reducing demand and supply while improving treatment—is still broadly right. But cocaine supply has increased, stronger synthetic opioids are appearing and ketamine use is rising. We need to check not just how many people get treatment, but whether it's the right treatment and whether it helps. I hope we can publish the update before the end of the year.

evidence.quote: She had three priorities: one was to reduce demand, one was to reduce supply, and one was to improve treatment. All of those things stand true
There is a lot more cocaine coming into the country
There are complex new synthetic opioids that are harder to detect and, in many cases, are much stronger than traditional drugs. We have increasing usage of things like ketamine.
we need to look at the quality of that treatment.
I hope that we will be able to do that before the end of the year

turns.speaker: Mr Kohler
turns.text: The existing strategy aimed to improve treatment, cut demand and cut supply. Haven't demand and the amount of drugs available gone in the wrong direction? Are you reconsidering the whole approach, or mainly updating it?

evidence.quote: Both the amount of demand and the amounts on the market have gone in the wrong direction, haven’t they?
rather than reconsidering the overall strategy, this is updating the overall strategy?

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones
turns.text: Treatment is more available, but we need to measure what happens to people after they receive it. We've done less well at reducing demand. This isn't a radical departure: we want to update priorities and respond to new risks. We're not planning to legalise drugs or change the law on cannabis.

evidence.quote: The £750 million-odd going into treatment has made a substantial difference to people’s ability to access treatment.
not just whether someone has turned up for their appointment, but what actually happened to that person
Where we have done less well—although there have been some public campaigns—is on anything to impact demand.
There is not a radical departure, but we want to update the strategy and prioritise a bit more.
We are not banning alcohol and we are not decriminalising cannabis.
We are not looking to change the legislative framework.

turns.speaker: Dr Prinsley
turns.text: We can't solve drug use just by arresting people. What are health and education services doing to explain the harm to young people and prevent them using drugs?

evidence.quote: What are we doing to educate young people about the dangers of drugs? What money are we spending on that?
you can’t arrest your way out of this problem; you have to somehow explain to people that this is harming them.

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones
turns.text: I agree. There's been a campaign warning young people about ketamine's lasting damage to the bladder, and schools do drugs education. If money were available, I'd like more public campaigns: people may not understand either the harm to users or how buying drugs supports violence.

evidence.quote: There has been one recently on ketamine to try to make sure that young people in particular who are using ketamine as a party drug recognise and understand the impact it can have on ruining your bladder
There is still a lot of work that goes on in the education field in terms of drugs and schools
if money were available, I would personally love to do more campaigns about drugs
people do not realise the harm they do, not just to people here but to millions of people around the world.

turns.speaker: Mr Kohler
turns.text: Turning to asset recovery: one estimate says just 0.3% of criminal assets are recovered. Do you recognise that figure, and what's stopping more money and property being taken from criminals?

evidence.quote: Spotlight on Corruption estimates that 0.3% of criminal assets are recovered. Do you recognise that figure, and is it fair?
Are there still problems in the process?

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones
turns.text: I haven't seen that estimate, but I wouldn't dismiss it. We recovered £345 million last year, which I imagine is only a fraction of what's possible. Court delays are one obstacle: a case might take three years to reach the point where assets can be recovered.

evidence.quote: I have not seen that figure, but I would not want to question it. We recovered £345 million last year, which I would imagine is a fraction of what we could do
There are problems in terms of court delays on getting to that, for sure. You might have a three-year delay

turns.speaker: Rod McLean
turns.text: The new strategy aims to make it easier to take criminal assets and prioritise compensation for victims. The amount recovered has risen: £345.3 million this year, 20% above last year. The National Audit Office is reviewing how well the recovery system works.

evidence.quote: prioritising compensation for victims and streamlining procedures through jurisprudence in the court to accelerate the recovery of assets.
it was £345.3 million this year, up 20% on last year
the National Audit Office is currently reviewing the effectiveness of the asset recovery system

turns.speaker: David Grahame
turns.text: It's also harder to find assets when criminals can hide them using cryptocurrency and other modern financial tools. The strategy includes new powers to seize crypto-assets and more investigators who can trace money.

evidence.quote: the complexity of the modern market—crypto, the ease of hiding things—and it is difficult to get into it.
new crypto-asset seizure powers, how you track those things, more financial investigators

chapters.title: Illegal goods sold online
chapters.takeaway: The Government is testing ways to find stolen goods online, but the Minister acknowledged gaps in its ability to prevent other illegal listings.

turns.speaker: Bell Ribeiro-Addy
turns.text: What are you doing about illegal goods sold through online marketplaces and social media? Can you require companies to act when goods are stolen, rather than just when the listings involve illegal knives?

evidence.quote: what action is the Home Office taking to tackle the sale of illegal goods through online marketplaces, particularly social media?
If they are illegal goods for other reasons, in that they have been stolen and so on, can you compel the companies in the same way?

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones
turns.text: We're funding an AI tool to look across second-hand sites for stolen goods, using details such as a tool's reference number. We've gone further on illegal knives, with powers to require companies to remove content. For other illegal listings, companies must have plans to prevent and remove them, but we don't necessarily have the enforcement tools we'd want.

evidence.quote: one of the pieces of work is looking across second-hand marketplaces to try to have an AI tool that can pick up stolen products.
you have a description of it and the reference number for it
We have introduced a law that basically enables us to force companies to remove content
if they do have something that is illegal, we do not necessarily have the tools to take action in the way that we would want to.
they have to take it down when it is seen

turns.speaker: Bell Ribeiro-Addy
turns.text: Would you consider warning buyers about counterfeit goods? They may not realise that these purchases can be harmful, as well as illegal. And are the current duties on online companies strong enough?

evidence.quote: would the Government consider a public awareness campaign to make consumers more aware of the negative consequences of buying these goods online?
Is there some sort of duty on the companies so that you can actually take action

turns.speaker: David Grahame
turns.text: Counterfeit goods can harm the buyer too, because of their quality or the substances in them. That's another reason to help people understand what they're buying.

evidence.quote: it can also be personally harmful to them in terms of the quality of the goods and the substances in them. It is about looking after yourself as well.

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones
turns.text: People may not realise how many illegal products are online, so there's probably more we could do to inform them. Ofcom can act when the Online Safety Act is broken, but we're asking whether its powers are enough and how to stop illegal listings appearing in the first place. There's more work to do, including on drugs sold online.

evidence.quote: I do not think that people recognise the quantity of illegal produce online, absolutely. You are right: we probably could do some work in that area
Ofcom has powers, if the Online Safety Act is breached, but there is a live question about whether those powers are enough
There is more to be done in this space, for sure, not least in the drugs area, where you have children buying drugs online with QR codes.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We want people to know that an online bargain that looks too good to be true may be funding organised crime and forced labour.

evidence.quote: if you see something that looks too good to be true, you are probably funding criminals, their criminal activities, forced labour and everything else that goes on behind it
